lessons.title: What is Economics?
lessons.focus: Defines economics, explains scarcity and choice, introduces basic terminology

data.title: What is Economics?
data.summary: Economics studies how people make choices when resources are limited. It introduces key ideas like scarcity, choice, and basic terminology.
objectives: Define economics in a single sentence
Explain the concept of scarcity with everyday examples
Describe how scarcity leads to choice and trade‑offs
Identify and use basic economic terms such as resource, want, need, and opportunity cost
data.prerequisites: No prior knowledge is required; students only need basic reading skills.
why: Understanding economics helps students see why they cannot have everything they want and how societies decide what to produce. This awareness influences personal budgeting, career choices, and civic participation.
The ideas of scarcity and choice are the foundation for all later topics, from markets to government policy. Grasping them early makes later concepts like supply and demand much easier to learn.

sections.heading: What is Economics?
sections.body:
Economics is the study of how people make choices when they have **limited resources** but **unlimited wants**.  
In plain words, it asks: *If we cannot have everything we want, how do we decide what to get and what to give up?*  

Why does this matter? Every day we face decisions – what to eat for breakfast, whether to buy a new video game or save the money for a concert ticket, how a city decides to build a park or a new road. All these choices involve using something that is scarce (like time, money, or land) to satisfy something we desire. By understanding the basic idea of economics, we can see the hidden logic behind these everyday decisions and make better ones ourselves.

> **Definition:** Economics is the study of how people, businesses, and societies allocate limited resources to satisfy unlimited wants.

### Resources, Wants, and Needs

- **Resources** are anything we can use to get something we want. They include **goods** (objects like a phone or a pair of shoes) and **services** (activities like a haircut or a doctor's visit). Resources also cover **factors of production**: land, labor (people’s work), capital (machines, tools), and entrepreneurship (the ability to combine the other factors into a product).  
- **Wants** are the things we would like to have. They are **unlimited** because there is always something new we could desire – a newer phone, a better vacation, a faster car.  
- **Needs** are the basic things required for survival, such as food, shelter, and clothing. While needs are essential, they are also a subset of wants; even after basic needs are met, people still want more.

Because resources are **limited** – there is only so much land, time, and money – we cannot satisfy every want. This mismatch creates the **core problem of economics**: scarcity.

### Scarcity: The Core Problem

Scarcity does not mean that something is rare in the sense of being exotic; it simply means that the amount available is **insufficient** to meet all desires at once. For example, a family may have $100 to spend on groceries this week. The grocery store offers many items, but the family cannot buy everything they like. They must decide which items give them the most satisfaction for the money they have.

When scarcity exists, **choice** becomes inevitable. Every choice involves a **trade‑off**: getting one thing means giving up something else. This is why economics focuses on **opportunity cost**, the value of the next best alternative that is forgone.

> **Note:** The opportunity cost of watching a movie is the time you could have spent studying, working, or exercising instead.

### Choice and Trade‑offs

Imagine you have two hours of free time after school. You could either **play video games** or **help a neighbor with yard work** for $10. If you choose to play games, the trade‑off is the $10 you could have earned. If you choose yard work, the trade‑off is the fun you miss while playing. Economics helps you weigh these alternatives by comparing the benefits you expect from each option.

Mathematically, we can write the decision rule as  

$$\text{Choose the option with the highest net benefit} = \text{Benefit} - \text{Opportunity Cost}$$  

If the net benefit of playing games is $5 (enjoyment value) – $0 (no money earned) = $5, and the net benefit of yard work is $10 (money) – $2 (lost enjoyment) = $8, the rational choice would be yard work.

> **In daily life:** When you decide to buy a snack instead of saving that money for a future purchase, the snack’s enjoyment is the benefit, and the future purchase you postpone is the opportunity cost.

### Basic Economic Terminology

- **Economics** – the study of choices under scarcity.  
- **Resource** – anything used to produce goods or services.  
- **Want** – any desire for a good or service; unlimited.  
- **Need** – a basic requirement for survival; a type of want.  
- **Scarcity** – the condition of limited resources versus unlimited wants.  
- **Opportunity cost** – the value of the next best alternative you give up when you make a choice.

Understanding these terms lets you read news about “budget deficits,” “inflation,” or “supply chain disruptions” with a clearer picture of the underlying choices people and governments are making.

> **Common mistake:** Thinking that scarcity only applies to money. In reality, time, attention, and even natural resources like clean water are all scarce.

### Putting It All Together

Economics starts with a simple observation: we cannot have everything we want because resources are limited. From this observation, the whole discipline builds a framework for analyzing how individuals, firms, and governments decide what to produce, how to produce it, and who gets the results. By recognizing that every decision involves a trade‑off, you become more aware of the hidden costs behind everyday choices.

> **Remember:** Whenever you face a decision, ask yourself: *What am I giving up?* That question is the heart of economics.

sections.heading: Resources, Wants, and Needs
sections.body:
Resources, wants, and needs are the three building blocks that help us understand every economic decision.  

First, think of **resources** as anything we own or can use to get something done. A resource can be a physical object, like a bicycle, a piece of land, or a computer. It can also be a non‑physical asset, such as a skill you have learned (for example, the ability to speak two languages) or time you can spend on an activity. In economics we call all of these “factors of production” because they are the inputs that allow us to produce goods and services.

> **Definition:** *Resources* are the things—both material and immaterial—that people, firms, or societies have at their disposal to produce goods and services.

Next come **wants**. A want is simply something you would like to have, even if you do not strictly need it to live. Wants are shaped by personal tastes, advertising, culture, and the choices of friends. One person might want the newest smartphone, while another might want a weekend trip to the mountains. Wants can be countless and can change quickly.

> **Note:** *Wants* are desires for goods or services that are not essential for survival; they are unlimited and vary from person to person.

Finally, there are **needs**. Needs are the basic items required for a healthy, functioning life. Economists usually list food, clean water, shelter, clothing, and basic health care as core needs. If any of these are missing, a person’s well‑being is directly threatened. Needs are relatively few and tend to be the same for almost everyone, regardless of culture or income level.

> **In daily life:** Imagine you have $20. Your **resources** are the $20 cash and the time you have after school. Your **needs** might be a sandwich for lunch and a bus ticket to get home. Your **wants** could be a new video game or a movie ticket. Because you only have $20, you must decide how to use your resources to satisfy both needs and wants.

Why does this distinction matter? Economics studies how limited resources are allocated to satisfy unlimited wants. Since resources are scarce (we will explore scarcity later), we cannot give everyone everything they want. Understanding what is a need versus a want helps people prioritize. For example, a family might choose to spend money on groceries (a need) before buying a new television (a want).

A simple way to see the relationship is with the equation:

$$
\text{Resources} = \text{Needs satisfied} + \text{Wants satisfied}
$$

This equation does not mean that every resource must be split exactly between needs and wants; it only shows that the total amount of resources you have is divided among the two categories of satisfaction. If you spend all your resources on wants, you may end up with unsatisfied needs, which can lead to problems like hunger or lack of shelter.

> **Common mistake:** Thinking that wants are the same as needs. Remember, wants are optional desires, while needs are essential for survival. Confusing the two can lead to poor budgeting decisions, such as buying a fancy gadget before paying the rent.

To practice, list three resources you have right now (e.g., a laptop, an hour of free time, a pair of shoes). Then write down one need and one want you could fulfill with each resource. Notice how the same resource can be used in different ways, but you must choose which use gives you the most benefit given your current situation.

By clearly separating resources, wants, and needs, you create a mental map that makes later topics—like scarcity, trade‑offs, and opportunity cost—much easier to grasp. Keep this framework in mind as you move forward; it will be the lens through which you view every economic choice.

sections.heading: Scarcity: The Core Problem
sections.body:
Scarcity means that there is not enough of something to satisfy every possible want.  
In economics we say that **resources** – the things we use to produce goods and services – are *finite*. Finite simply means “limited in amount”. Because the amount of resources is limited, we cannot give everyone everything they would like. This basic fact is called **scarcity**, and it is the starting point for every economic decision.

> **Definition:** *Scarcity* is the condition that resources are limited while human wants are unlimited.

Why does scarcity matter? If we knew that every desire could be met without any limits, we would never need to think about choices, prices, or trade‑offs. In the real world, however, we must decide how to use the little we have. Understanding scarcity helps us ask the right questions: *What should we produce? How much should we produce? Who gets it?* These questions form the core of economic analysis.

Think of a simple everyday example: **time**. Each day we have only 24 hours. Suppose you want to study for a test, play video games, and help with chores. Because the 24 hours are fixed, you cannot do all three activities for the whole day. You must choose how to split your time. The limited amount of time creates scarcity, and your choices create *trade‑offs* – gaining more of one activity means giving up some of another.

Another familiar illustration is **money**. Imagine you receive a $20 allowance. You would like to buy a new video game that costs $30, go to the movies ($12), and buy a snack ($5). Since you only have $20, you cannot afford everything. You must decide which items give you the most satisfaction and which you are willing to forgo. The $20 is a scarce resource that forces you to prioritize.

When we talk about scarcity, we also use the term **opportunity cost**. This is the value of the next best alternative you give up when you make a choice. In the time example, if you spend an extra hour studying, the opportunity cost is the hour of video‑game play you lose. In the money example, if you buy the snack, the opportunity cost is part of the movie ticket you can no longer afford.

> **Note:** The *opportunity cost* is not always measured in dollars; it can be measured in time, enjoyment, or any other thing you value.

Economists often write a simple relationship to remind us of the trade‑off:

$$
\text{Total Resources} = \text{Used Resources} + \text{Unused Resources}
$$

If the total amount of a resource (like money or time) is fixed, increasing the part we *use* automatically reduces the part that stays *unused*. This equation captures the essence of scarcity: using more of a limited resource leaves less for other purposes.

> **In daily life:** When you plan a weekend, you have a limited number of hours. Deciding to watch a movie means you have fewer hours left for a hike. Recognizing this trade‑off helps you allocate your time in a way that matches your priorities.

A common mistake is to think that scarcity only applies to “big” things like oil or land. In fact, scarcity is present in every decision, no matter how small. Even choosing between two flavors of ice cream involves a tiny amount of scarcity – you can only eat one scoop at a time.

> **Common mistake:** Assuming that because a resource feels abundant today, it will stay abundant forever. Resources can become scarcer due to changes in supply, technology, or preferences, so the need to make choices never disappears.

Remember, scarcity does not mean we cannot have anything at all; it simply means we must make choices. By recognizing that resources are limited, we become better at evaluating alternatives, setting priorities, and understanding why prices exist. This awareness is the first step toward thinking like an economist.

sections.heading: Choice and Trade‑offs
sections.body:
When we say that resources are limited, we also mean that we cannot have everything we want at the same time.  
Because of this limitation, every person, family, business, and government must **choose** what to do and **give up** something else. This act of deciding between alternatives is called a *trade‑off*.

> **Definition:** A **trade‑off** is a situation in which gaining one thing requires losing something else.

Why does this happen? Imagine you have a fixed amount of time each day—say, 24 hours. If you spend 2 hours studying for a math test, those 2 hours are no longer available to watch a movie, play a sport, or help a sibling with homework. The scarcity of time forces you to pick one activity and sacrifice the others. The same logic works for money, land, raw materials, and even natural resources like water.

### The idea of opportunity cost

When we make a choice, the value of the next best alternative that we **did not** choose is called the *opportunity cost*. It tells us what we are giving up.

> **Note:** **Opportunity cost** = the benefit you would have received from the best alternative you gave up.

For example, suppose you have $10 and you can either buy a book or a video game. If you buy the book, the opportunity cost is the enjoyment you would have gotten from playing the video game. If you buy the video game, the opportunity cost is the knowledge you would have gained from reading the book. The opportunity cost is not just the price of the item you didn’t pick; it is the *value* you place on that missed option.

### How trade‑offs shape decisions

1. **Individual level** – A student decides how many hours to study versus how many hours to work a part‑time job. The trade‑off is between higher grades (future earnings) and current income (money to spend now).  
2. **Family level** – A family with a limited budget must decide whether to spend more on health care or on a family vacation. The trade‑off involves immediate well‑being versus leisure and memories.  
3. **Societal level** – A government with a fixed tax revenue must allocate funds among education, defense, and infrastructure. Each allocation creates a trade‑off: more money for schools means less for roads or the military.

In each case, the decision‑maker looks at the *marginal* benefit (the extra gain from one more unit of something) and the *marginal* cost (the extra loss from giving up the next best use). The goal is to choose the option where the marginal benefit exceeds the marginal cost, or at least where the benefit of the chosen option is greater than the opportunity cost.

### Simple equation for opportunity cost

If we let  

$$\text{Opportunity Cost} = \text{Benefit of Best Alternative Not Chosen}$$  

then the decision rule can be written as  

$$\text{Choose Option A if } \text{Benefit}_A > \text{Opportunity Cost}_A.$$

### Why understanding trade‑offs matters

Recognizing trade‑offs helps us make more informed choices. It prevents us from focusing only on the immediate gain and ignoring what we lose elsewhere. It also clarifies why policies that look “free” often have hidden costs. For instance, a tax cut may boost disposable income for some people, but the opportunity cost could be reduced funding for public schools or hospitals.

> **In daily life:** When you decide to eat a candy bar instead of an apple, the opportunity cost is the extra vitamins and fiber you would have gotten from the apple.

> **Common mistake:** Thinking that the price you pay in money is the only cost. True cost includes the value of the next best thing you give up.

> **Remember:** Every choice involves a trade‑off, and the opportunity cost tells you what you are really giving up. By comparing benefits to opportunity costs, you can choose the option that gives you the most overall satisfaction.

sections.heading: Basic Economic Terminology
sections.body:
Economics is the study of how people use limited resources to satisfy unlimited wants.  
To talk about this clearly we need a few basic words. Each word will be introduced slowly, with a simple example, so you can see how they fit together.

A **resource** is anything that can be used to produce something else.  
> **Definition:** *Resource* – a supply of land, labor, capital, or entrepreneurship that helps create goods and services.  

Think of a kitchen. The stove, the pots, the chef’s skill, and even the electricity are all resources. Without them you could not make a meal.

When a resource is turned into something you can own or use, we call the result a **good**.  
> **In daily life:** *Good* – a physical item like a smartphone, a book, or a pair of shoes that you can touch and keep.  

If the result is an activity that helps people but cannot be stored, it is a **service**.  
> **In daily life:** *Service* – a haircut, a doctor’s visit, or a bus ride; you receive the benefit, but there is no object to hold.  

People have **wants** and **needs**. A *need* is something essential for survival, such as food, water, and shelter. A *want* is something that makes life nicer but is not essential, like a video game or a new car.  
> **Note:** Economists treat both wants and needs as “desires” that drive economic activity; the distinction matters when we discuss scarcity.

**Scarcity** is the core problem in economics. It means that resources are limited while wants are unlimited. Because we cannot have everything, we must decide how to allocate what we have.  
> **Remember:** *Scarcity* forces us to make choices.

A **choice** is the decision to use a resource in one way rather than another. Every choice involves a **trade‑off**: when you pick one option, you give up another. The value of the next best alternative you give up is called the **opportunity cost**.  

For example, suppose you have $10 and you can either buy a book or go to the movies. If you choose the book, the opportunity cost is the enjoyment you would have gotten from the movie. In symbols, we can write  

$$\text{Opportunity Cost} = \text{Value of the next best alternative not chosen}$$  

Understanding opportunity cost helps you compare options and pick the one that gives the most benefit for the resources you have.

All of these decisions usually happen in a **market**. A market is any place—physical or virtual—where buyers and sellers meet to exchange goods and services. Prices in a market signal how scarce a good is and help allocate resources efficiently.  

> **Common mistake:** Thinking that a market always guarantees the best outcome. Markets work well when many buyers and sellers interact, but they can fail if information is missing or if some people have too much power.

Putting the terms together, you can see the flow: resources → (through production) → goods and services → (through markets) → choices and trade‑offs → opportunity costs.  

When you hear an economist talk about “the scarcity of water,” they mean that the amount of clean water (a resource) is limited compared to how many people want or need it. The market will set a price, and each person will decide whether to buy water, conserve it, or find an alternative, weighing the opportunity cost of each option.

By mastering these words, you gain the language to describe everyday economic situations—whether you are budgeting your allowance, deciding what to study, or understanding why a new smartphone costs a lot. The same ideas apply to big‑scale issues like government budgeting or global trade, because the same principles of scarcity, choice, and opportunity cost operate at every level.

sections.heading: Putting It All Together
sections.body:
Imagine you have a limited amount of money, time, or any other resource. Because you cannot have everything you might want, you must decide **what to do with what you have**. This simple idea is the heart of economics, and it links three key concepts: **scarcity**, **choice**, and **opportunity cost**.

> **Definition:** *Scarcity* means that resources (like money, time, raw materials, or even attention) are limited while human wants are unlimited.  

Because resources are scarce, you cannot satisfy every desire at once. This forces you to make **choices**—deciding which wants to fulfill and which to postpone or ignore.

> **Note:** A *choice* is any decision you make when faced with alternatives. Every choice involves a *trade‑off*: you give up something in order to get something else.

When you choose one option, you automatically give up the next best alternative. The value of that forgone alternative is called the **opportunity cost**.

> **Definition:** *Opportunity cost* is the benefit you miss out on when you pick one option over another. It is not just the money you spend, but also the enjoyment, time, or other benefits you could have received from the alternative.

### How the three ideas fit together

1. **Scarcity creates the need to choose.**  
   If you have $10 and want to buy a book that costs $8 and a snack that costs $4, you cannot afford both. The limited $10 forces you to pick one.

2. **Choice leads to a trade‑off.**  
   Suppose you decide to buy the book. The trade‑off is that you cannot buy the snack. You have exchanged the snack for the book.

3. **Opportunity cost measures the trade‑off.**  
   The opportunity cost of buying the book is the enjoyment you would have gotten from the snack. If the snack would have given you $3 of satisfaction, then the opportunity cost of the book is $3 of satisfaction.

In formula form, we can write:

$$
\text{Opportunity Cost} = \text{Value of the Best Alternative Not Chosen}
$$

This equation reminds us that opportunity cost is always measured against the *best* alternative you gave up, not just any alternative.

### Everyday examples

- **Time management:** You have two hours free after school. You could study for a test or play video games. If you study, the opportunity cost is the fun and relaxation you miss from gaming. If you game, the opportunity cost is the higher test score you might have earned.

- **Budgeting:** A family has a fixed monthly grocery budget. Choosing to buy organic vegetables may mean they cannot afford a weekend outing. The opportunity cost of the organic food is the missed family outing.

- **Energy use:** A household decides whether to run the air conditioner all day or keep windows open. Running the AC keeps the house cool but costs electricity; the opportunity cost is the extra money that could have been saved or spent elsewhere.

### Why this matters

Understanding the link between scarcity, choice, and opportunity cost helps you think clearly about everyday decisions. It forces you to ask:

- *What am I giving up?*  
- *Is the benefit I gain worth the cost of what I lose?*  

When you habitually consider opportunity cost, you become better at allocating limited resources—whether money, time, or effort—toward the things that matter most to you.

> **In daily life:** Whenever you decide to spend an hour on homework instead of watching TV, you are weighing the opportunity cost of missing out on entertainment against the benefit of better grades.

> **Common mistake:** Many people think “cost” only means money. Remember, opportunity cost includes any benefit you forgo, such as time, enjoyment, or future possibilities.

By seeing how scarcity forces choice and how every choice has an opportunity cost, you can apply economic thinking to everything from small personal decisions to big policy debates. This simple framework turns a complex world into a series of understandable trade‑offs, helping you make smarter, more intentional choices.

sections.heading: Check Your Understanding
sections.body:
**Check Your Understanding**

Think of the ideas you have just learned as tools you can use to look at everyday situations. Below are short reflection questions that will help you see whether you can apply the key definitions and concepts of economics. Read each question carefully, pause, and try to answer in your own words before checking the hint that follows.

> **Definition:** *Economics* is the study of how people make choices when resources are limited.

1. **What is the main problem that economics tries to solve?**  
   *Hint:* Imagine you have only $10 but want to buy a book, a snack, and a movie ticket. Which part of economics does this situation illustrate?

> **In daily life:** *Scarcity* means there is not enough of something to satisfy everyone’s wants.

2. **Identify a resource in your school that is scarce.**  
   Explain why it is scarce and give one example of a trade‑off that the school must make because of this scarcity.

> **Note:** A *trade‑off* occurs when choosing more of one thing means having less of another.

3. **Your family wants to go on a weekend trip. List two different things they might have to give up to afford the trip.**  
   Describe how each choice reflects a trade‑off.

> **Common mistake:** Thinking that “needs” and “wants” are the same. Needs are essential for survival; wants are anything extra we would like to have.

4. **Pick an item you bought last month. Classify it as a need or a want, and explain why you placed it in that category.**  
   How would your answer change if you had no money left after buying it?

> **Remember:** *Opportunity cost* is the value of the next best alternative you give up when you make a choice.

5. **You have an hour after school. You could either study for a test or play video games. What is the opportunity cost of studying?**  
   Write a short sentence that shows you understand the concept.

Now try a short scenario that ties several ideas together.

6. **Scenario:** The city council has $5 million to improve public services. They can either build a new park or repair old roads.  
   - List the *resources* involved.  
   - Explain the *scarcity* issue.  
   - Identify at least two *trade‑offs* the council faces.  
   - State the *opportunity cost* of choosing the park.

Finally, test your ability to use economic language in a real‑world observation.

7. **Observation:** Look at the news headline “Rising prices for fresh fruit.”  
   - Which economic term describes the rise in prices?  
   - What might be a *scarcity* reason behind this change?  
   - Suggest one *choice* a household could make in response, and describe the *trade‑off* involved.

Take a moment to write down your answers. When you feel confident, compare them with a classmate or discuss them with your teacher. The goal is not just to recall definitions, but to see how economics helps you think clearly about everyday decisions.

practice.q: Define economics in one sentence.
practice.a: Economics is the study of how people and societies use limited resources to satisfy unlimited wants and needs.

practice.q: Why is scarcity considered the core problem in economics?
practice.a: Scarcity means resources are limited while wants are unlimited, so choices must be made about how to allocate those resources.

practice.q: Explain the difference between a need and a want, and give an example of each.
practice.a: A need is something essential for survival, such as food or shelter. A want is something desired but not essential, like a new video game. For example, water is a need; a smartphone upgrade is a want.

practice.q: How does the concept of trade‑offs relate to the idea of opportunity cost? Illustrate with a simple example.
practice.a: Trade‑offs occur when choosing one option means giving up another. The opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative that is forgone. Example: If you spend an hour studying economics, the trade‑off is not spending that hour playing basketball; the opportunity cost is the enjoyment and exercise you miss from basketball.

practice.q: A community has 100 acres of land, 50 workers, and $10,000 in capital. They can produce either wheat or clothing. Explain how scarcity forces the community to make a production choice and describe the trade‑offs involved.
practice.a: The community’s resources (land, labor, capital) are limited, so they cannot produce unlimited amounts of both wheat and clothing. They must decide how much land, how many workers, and how much capital to allocate to each product. If they allocate more resources to wheat, they will produce more food but less clothing, and vice versa. The trade‑off is the amount of clothing forgone when producing extra wheat, measured by the opportunity cost in terms of clothing units.

practice.q: Identify and define three basic economic terms covered in this lesson, then explain how they are interconnected in the decision‑making process.
practice.a:
Three terms are:
1. **Resources** – the inputs (land, labor, capital, entrepreneurship) used to produce goods and services.
2. **Scarcity** – the condition of limited resources relative to unlimited wants.
3. **Choice** – the act of selecting among alternatives due to scarcity.
These are interconnected because scarcity of resources forces individuals and societies to make choices about how to use those resources. Every choice involves a trade‑off, reflecting the relationship among the three concepts.

data.recap: Economics studies how people, firms, and societies allocate limited resources to satisfy unlimited wants. The core problem is scarcity, which forces choices and trade‑offs. When a choice is made, the next best alternative that is given up is the opportunity cost. Understanding these ideas helps us analyze everyday decisions.

key_terms.meaning: The study of how people allocate limited resources to satisfy unlimited wants.
Anything—land, labor, capital, skills, or time—used to produce goods or services.
The condition that resources are limited while human wants are unlimited.
When gaining one thing requires giving up something else.
The value of the next best alternative that is forgone when a choice is made.
A tangible product that can be owned, such as a phone or a book.
An intangible activity that benefits people, like teaching or haircuts.
A decision made between two or more alternatives.

quiz.q: What is the main problem that economics tries to solve?
options: How to satisfy unlimited wants with limited resources
quiz.why: Economics focuses on allocating scarce resources to meet endless wants.

quiz.q: Which of the following is an example of a resource?
options: A wish for a new phone
quiz.why: A bicycle is a tangible asset that can be used to produce or provide services.

quiz.q: If you spend $5 on a snack, what is the opportunity cost?
options: The movie ticket you could have bought
quiz.why: The movie ticket is the next best alternative you gave up.

quiz.q: What does scarcity imply?
options: Resources are limited while wants are unlimited
quiz.why: Scarcity means limited resources versus unlimited wants.

quiz.q: Choosing to study for an hour means you give up:
options: A chance to watch a video
quiz.why: Time spent studying cannot be used for sleep or video, illustrating a trade‑off.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a service?
quiz.why: A haircut is an activity that provides benefit but cannot be stored.

lessons.title: Supply and Demand Basics
lessons.focus: Shows how prices are set by supply and demand, includes simple graphs

data.title: Supply and Demand Basics
data.summary: Students learn how prices are determined by the interaction of supply and demand and how to read simple supply‑demand graphs.
objectives: Explain what supply and demand curves represent
Identify equilibrium price and quantity on a graph
Describe how shifts in supply or demand affect price
Calculate the new equilibrium after a shift
Interpret real‑world price changes using the model
data.prerequisites: Students should know basic arithmetic and be familiar with the idea of a market where buyers and sellers meet.
why: Understanding supply and demand helps people predict how prices of everyday items—like smartphones or groceries—will change when something in the market changes, such as a new technology or a bad harvest.
Businesses use the same ideas to decide how much to produce and at what price to sell, while governments look at them when designing policies that affect the economy.

sections.heading: 1. What is Demand?
sections.body:
Demand is simply the amount of a product that people want to buy at different prices.  
Think of it as a “willingness‑and‑ability” meter: when the price is low, more people are willing and able to purchase the good; when the price is high, fewer people are willing or able to buy it.  

> **Definition:** *Demand* is the relationship between the price of a good and the quantity of that good that consumers are willing and able to purchase during a specific period of time.

Why does this relationship matter?  It helps businesses decide how much to produce and at what price to sell, and it helps governments understand how changes in taxes or subsidies might affect the market.

### The demand curve

Economists draw a graph to show demand visually. On the horizontal axis (the x‑axis) we put **quantity demanded** – the number of units people want to buy. On the vertical axis (the y‑axis) we put **price** – how much each unit costs.  

When we plot several price‑quantity pairs that we observe in the real world, the points usually line up in a downward‑sloping shape. Connecting the points gives us the **demand curve**. The downward slope means that as price falls, the quantity demanded rises, and vice‑versa.

> **Note:** The demand curve is a *model* – a simplified picture that captures the main idea, not every tiny detail of real markets.

### The law of demand

The regular pattern that the demand curve shows is called the **law of demand**. It states:

> When the price of a good falls, the quantity demanded of that good rises, **ceteris paribus** (all other things being equal).  
> When the price rises, the quantity demanded falls, **ceteris paribus**.

The phrase *ceteris paribus* is Latin for “all other things being the same.” It reminds us that the law of demand holds only when other factors that could affect demand – such as consumer income, tastes, or the price of related goods – do not change at the same time.

#### Why does the law work?

Two main reasons explain the downward slope:

1. **Substitution effect** – If the price of apples goes down, apples become cheaper compared with oranges. People will buy more apples and fewer oranges.
2. **Income effect** – A lower price means that the same amount of money can buy more apples, effectively increasing the buyer’s purchasing power. This extra “real income” encourages them to buy more.

Both effects push the quantity demanded upward when price drops.

### Putting numbers on the idea

Suppose a survey shows the following data for a popular video game:

| Price per copy ($) | Quantity demanded (thousands) |
|--------------------|------------------------------|
| 60                 | 2                            |
| 50                 | 3                            |
| 40                 | 5                            |
| 30                 | 8                            |

If we plot these points, we get a straight line that slopes downwards. For many simple cases we can write the demand relationship as a linear equation:

$$ Q_d = a - bP $$

where  

- $Q_d$ = quantity demanded,  
- $P$ = price,  
- $a$ and $b$ are positive constants that depend on the product and the market.

In the example above, a possible equation is $Q_d = 10 - 0.13P$. When $P = 60$, $Q_d = 10 - 0.13(60) = 2$ thousand copies, matching the data.

> **In daily life:** When a coffee shop offers a “buy one, get one free” deal, the price per cup effectively drops, so more people line up to buy coffee – a clear illustration of the law of demand.

Understanding demand is the first step toward analyzing how markets work. Once we know how consumers respond to price changes, we can later explore how producers respond (supply) and how the two forces meet at the **equilibrium** price and quantity.

sections.heading: 2. What is Supply?
sections.body:
Supply is the amount of a good or service that producers are willing and able to sell at different prices during a certain time period.  
Think of a farmer who grows strawberries. If the market price of strawberries is low, the farmer may decide to sell only a few baskets because the profit is small. If the price rises, the farmer can earn more from each basket, so he is ready to bring more baskets to the market. This intuitive idea—that higher prices encourage producers to supply more—is called the **law of supply**.

> **Definition:** *Supply* is the relationship between the price of a good and the quantity that producers are willing to sell, holding everything else constant.

Why does the law of supply hold?  
Producers aim to cover their costs (seeds, labor, equipment) and earn a profit. When the selling price goes up, the revenue from each unit rises while the cost of producing each unit stays roughly the same. The extra revenue makes it worthwhile to increase production, perhaps by using more labor or better technology. Conversely, if the price falls, the extra revenue disappears, and producing the same amount may no longer cover costs, so producers cut back.

### The Supply Curve

We draw the supply relationship on a graph called the **supply curve**.  
- The horizontal axis (x‑axis) shows *quantity supplied* (how many units are offered).  
- The vertical axis (y‑axis) shows *price* (how much each unit sells for).  

When we plot several price‑quantity pairs that follow the law of supply, the points line up in an upward‑sloping shape. The upward slope tells us that as price increases, quantity supplied also increases.

> **Note:** The supply curve assumes that other factors—like technology, input prices, and taxes—stay the same. These are called *ceteris paribus* conditions (Latin for “all other things equal”).

#### Mathematical representation

If we assume a simple linear relationship, we can write supply as  

$$ Q_s = a + bP $$  

where  

- $Q_s$ = quantity supplied,  
- $P$ = price,  
- $a$ = intercept (quantity supplied when price is zero, often negative or zero),  
- $b$ = slope (how much quantity changes when price changes).  

Because the law of supply says quantity rises when price rises, the slope $b$ is **positive** ($b>0$).

### Worked Example 1 (Level: Introductory)

**Example 1 (Level): Linear supply of notebooks**  

A school supplies company sells notebooks. Its supply relationship is given by  

$$ Q_s = -20 + 5P $$  

where $Q_s$ is the number of notebooks (in dozens) the company is willing to sell each week, and $P$ is the price per dozen in dollars.  

1. **Find the quantity supplied when the price is \$8 per dozen.**  
   Substitute $P = 8$ into the equation:  

   $$ Q_s = -20 + 5(8) $$  

2. **Calculate the result.**  
   $$ Q_s = -20 + 40 = 20 $$  

3. **Interpret the answer.**  
   The company will supply 20 dozens of notebooks each week when the price is \$8 per dozen.

**Answer:** 20 dozens of notebooks per week.

This example shows how a higher price ($8) leads to a positive quantity supplied (20 dozens), consistent with the law of supply.

### Shifts of the Supply Curve

The supply curve can move left or right when something other than price changes. These are called **supply shifts**. Common reasons include:

- **Input price changes:** If the cost of wood (an input for pencils) rises, producing pencils becomes more expensive, so at every price the firm will supply fewer pencils. The curve shifts **left** (upward).
- **Technology improvements:** A new machine that speeds up production lowers the cost per unit, so firms can supply more at each price. The curve shifts **right** (downward).
- **Number of sellers:** More firms entering the market increase total market supply, shifting the curve right.

> **In daily life:** Imagine a bakery that makes cupcakes. If the price of flour goes up, the bakery may bake fewer cupcakes at any given cupcake price, moving its supply curve left. If a new oven lets the bakery bake twice as fast, the supply curve moves right because it can make more cupcakes for the same price.

### Why the Supply Curve Matters

Understanding the supply curve helps us predict how markets respond to changes. Policymakers use it to estimate the effect of taxes, subsidies, or regulations. Businesses use it to decide how much to produce when market prices change.

> **Remember:** The *law of supply* tells us the direction (upward slope) of the supply curve; *shifts* tell us how the whole curve moves when non‑price factors change.

### Quick Checklist

- Supply = relationship between price and quantity producers are willing to sell.  
- Law of supply: higher price → higher quantity supplied (upward‑sloping curve).  
- Linear supply can be written $Q_s = a + bP$ with $b>0$.  
- Shifts occur when factors other than price change (input costs, technology, number of sellers).  

With these ideas, you can now read a supply curve, write its equation, and see how real‑world events move it. In the next section we will combine supply with demand to find the market **equilibrium** price and quantity.

sections.heading: 3. Finding Equilibrium
sections.body:
When buyers and sellers meet in a market, each side has its own “plan” for how much to trade at different prices.  
The **demand curve** shows how many units consumers are willing to buy at each possible price, while the **supply curve** shows how many units producers are willing to sell.  

If we draw both curves on the same graph—price on the vertical axis and quantity on the horizontal axis—the point where the two lines cross is called the **equilibrium**. At this point the amount that buyers want to buy exactly equals the amount that sellers want to sell. No one is left with unsold goods, and no one is forced to pay more or receive less than they are willing to.

> **Definition:** *Equilibrium price* (also called market‑clearing price) is the price at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied.  
> **Note:** The corresponding *equilibrium quantity* is the amount bought and sold at that price.

Why does this matter?  
- **Stability:** If the price is above equilibrium, there will be a surplus (more goods than people want). Sellers will lower their price to get rid of excess stock, pushing the price down toward equilibrium.  
- **Scarcity:** If the price is below equilibrium, there will be a shortage (more people want the good than is available). Buyers will compete, bidding the price up until the shortage disappears.  

Think of a busy coffee shop in the morning. Suppose the shop sets the price of a latte at \$5, but at that price only 30 customers line up while the baristas can make 50 drinks per hour. The shop has **excess supply** (a surplus). To fill the empty seats, the manager might drop the price to \$4.5, attracting more customers. After a few adjustments, the price settles at a level where the number of customers who want a latte exactly matches the number the baristas can prepare—that is the equilibrium.

### Solving for equilibrium algebraically  

When the demand and supply relationships are given as equations, we can find the equilibrium by setting **quantity demanded (Qd)** equal to **quantity supplied (Qs)** and solving for the price (P). The steps are:

1. Write the demand equation: $Q_d = f(P)$  
2. Write the supply equation: $Q_s = g(P)$  
3. Set them equal: $f(P) = g(P)$  
4. Solve the resulting equation for $P$ (the equilibrium price).  
5. Substitute that price back into either the demand or supply equation to get the equilibrium quantity $Q$.

#### Worked example  

**Example 2 (Easy): Finding equilibrium for a linear market**  
A market has a demand curve $Q_d = 100 - 2P$ and a supply curve $Q_s = 20 + 3P$. Find the equilibrium price and quantity.

1. **Set demand equal to supply**  
   $$100 - 2P = 20 + 3P$$  

2. **Collect the $P$ terms on one side**  
   $$100 - 20 = 3P + 2P$$  
   $$80 = 5P$$  

3. **Solve for the price**  
   $$P = \frac{80}{5} = 16$$  

4. **Find the quantity by plugging $P = 16$ into either equation** (use the demand equation)  
   $$Q = 100 - 2(16) = 100 - 32 = 68$$  

**Answer:** The equilibrium price is **\$16** and the equilibrium quantity is **68 units**. At this price, buyers want exactly 68 units and sellers are ready to supply exactly 68 units.

### Interpreting the result  

The numbers tell us two things:

- **Price signal:** \$16 is the market‑clearing price. If the shop tried to charge \$20, it would sell fewer than 68 lattes, leaving unsold coffee. If it charged \$12, it would run out of coffee because more than 68 people would want a latte.
- **Quantity signal:** 68 units is the amount the market can sustain without creating a surplus or shortage. Producers can plan their resources (beans, labor) around this level.

> **In daily life:** When a popular video game console launches, the initial price may be high because demand exceeds supply. As more units are produced, the price falls until it reaches the equilibrium where most people who want the console can buy it and the manufacturer is selling all the units it makes.

### What if the curves are not straight lines?  

The same principle works for any shape of demand and supply curves, as long as they intersect. For curved lines, we may need algebraic manipulation or, in more complex cases, calculus or numerical methods. The core idea—*equate quantity demanded and quantity supplied*—remains unchanged.

### Quick checklist for finding equilibrium  

> **Remember:**  
> 1. Write down the two equations clearly.  
> 2. Set them equal to each other (because at equilibrium $Q_d = Q_s$).  
> 3. Solve step‑by‑step, keeping track of units.  
> 4. Verify by substituting the price back into both equations; the two quantities should match.

Understanding equilibrium gives you a powerful tool: you can predict how a market will respond when something changes—like a tax, a new technology, or a shift in consumer tastes. The next sections will show how those changes move the curves and create new equilibrium points.

sections.heading: 4. Demand Shifts
sections.body:
When we talk about a **demand shift**, we mean that the whole demand curve moves to the left or to the right.  
The curve does not just slide up or down; it changes its position because something other than the price of the good has changed.  

> **Definition:** A *demand shift* occurs when a factor other than the good’s own price changes, causing consumers to want to buy a different amount at every possible price.  

The most common reasons for a shift are:

| Factor | How it changes demand |
|--------|----------------------|
| **Income** (how much money people earn) | If people earn more, they can afford to buy more of many goods, so the demand curve moves **right** (increase). If income falls, the curve moves **left** (decrease). |
| **Tastes and preferences** (what people like) | A new fashion, a health study, or a popular movie can make a product more attractive, shifting demand right. The opposite makes it shift left. |
| **Prices of related goods** | If the price of a substitute (a good used instead) falls, demand for our good falls (left). If the price of a complement (a good used together) falls, demand for our good rises (right). |
| **Expectations** (what people think will happen) | Expecting higher future prices makes people buy now, shifting demand right today. |
| **Number of buyers** | More buyers → right shift; fewer buyers → left shift. |

Why does this matter?  
If the demand curve moves, the point where it meets the supply curve – the **equilibrium** – also moves. That means the market price and the quantity sold will change. Understanding the direction and size of the shift helps businesses decide how much to produce and helps policymakers predict inflationary pressures.

> **In daily life:** When a new smartphone is announced, many people expect it to be the best device. Even before it is released, they may buy the current model, pushing its demand curve to the right and raising its price.

### Step‑by‑step: From a shift to a new equilibrium

1. **Write the original demand equation.**  
   In our basic market we used  
   $$Q_d = 100 - 2P$$  
   where \(Q_d\) is quantity demanded and \(P\) is price.

2. **Identify the factor that changes.**  
   Suppose consumer income rises. Empirical data tells us that for this good, a rise in income makes the intercept (the number that stands alone when \(P = 0\)) increase from 100 to 120, while the slope \(-2\) stays the same. The new demand equation becomes  
   $$Q_d' = 120 - 2P$$

3. **Keep the supply equation unchanged** (unless the problem says otherwise).  
   Our supply curve is still  
   $$Q_s = 20 + P$$

4. **Find the new equilibrium** by setting the new demand equal to supply:  
   $$120 - 2P = 20 + P$$  

5. **Solve for \(P\)** (price). Then plug that price back into either equation to get the new quantity.

The algebra is straightforward, but let us walk through it carefully in a worked example.

---

**Example 3 (Medium): Income rise shifts demand to \(Q_d = 120 - 2P\)**  
Calculate the new equilibrium price and quantity.

1. **Set the new demand equal to supply.**  
   $$120 - 2P = 20 + P$$  

2. **Collect the \(P\) terms on one side.**  
   Add \(2P\) to both sides:  
   $$120 = 20 + 3P$$  

3. **Isolate \(P\).**  
   Subtract 20 from both sides:  
   $$100 = 3P$$  
   Divide by 3:  
   $$P = \frac{100}{3} \approx 33.33$$  

4. **Find the equilibrium quantity** by substituting \(P\) back into either the demand or supply equation (use the simpler supply equation).  
   $$Q_s = 20 + P = 20 + 33.33 = 53.33$$  

**Answer:** The new equilibrium price is about **\$33.33**, and the equilibrium quantity is about **53 units**.  

> **Remember:** When demand shifts right, both equilibrium price **and** quantity usually rise (provided the supply curve slopes upward as usual).

### What if the shift is left?

If income fell instead, the demand intercept would drop, for example to 80, giving  
$$Q_d'' = 80 - 2P$$  
Repeating the same steps:

1. Set \(80 - 2P = 20 + P\).  
2. Solve: \(80 = 20 + 3P \Rightarrow 60 = 3P \Rightarrow P = 20\).  
3. Quantity: \(Q_s = 20 + 20 = 40\).

So the equilibrium price falls to \$20 and quantity to 40 units. This illustrates the opposite effect of a leftward shift.

> **Common mistake:** Forgetting that the *slope* of the demand curve stays the same when only income changes. Only the intercept moves; changing the slope would mean a different kind of factor (like a change in how price‑sensitive consumers are).

### Quick checklist for a demand shift problem

- **Identify** which non‑price factor changed (income, taste, etc.).  
- **Adjust** the demand equation accordingly (usually the intercept).  
- **Leave** the supply equation unchanged unless the problem says otherwise.  
- **Set** the new demand equal to supply and **solve** for price first, then quantity.  

> **Note:** The direction of the shift tells you instantly whether price and quantity will rise or fall, but you still need the algebra to know the exact new numbers.

By mastering these steps, you can predict how real‑world events—like a rise in wages or a new health craze—will move market outcomes. This skill is the foundation for later topics such as tax incidence, price controls, and welfare analysis.

sections.heading: 5. Supply Shifts
sections.body:
Supply does not stay still.  
When something changes the cost of making a good, or a new way of producing it appears, the whole **supply curve** moves.  
The curve itself is the picture of “how much producers are willing to sell at each price”.  
If producers can make the product cheaper, they are willing to sell more at every price, so the curve shifts **rightward**.  
If it becomes more expensive to produce, the curve shifts **leftward**.

> **Definition:** *Supply shift* – a movement of the entire supply curve to the right (increase) or to the left (decrease) caused by a change in production costs, technology, taxes, or the number of sellers.

Why does this matter?  
The market price and quantity are found where the supply curve meets the demand curve.  
When the supply curve moves, the meeting point – the **equilibrium** – also moves.  
Understanding the direction and size of the shift helps us predict whether prices will fall or rise and whether the amount bought and sold will grow or shrink.

### Everyday comparison  
Think of a bakery that bakes bread.  
If the bakery buys a new oven that bakes twice as many loaves per hour, the baker can produce more bread for the same amount of money.  
That is like the supply curve moving right.  
Customers still want the same amount of bread at each price, but now the bakery can offer more, so the market price tends to drop and the total quantity sold rises.

### What can shift supply?

| Factor | Effect on supply curve |
|--------|------------------------|
| Lower input prices (e.g., cheaper flour) | Rightward shift (increase) |
| Higher input prices (e.g., expensive wheat) | Leftward shift (decrease) |
| Technological improvement (e.g., faster oven) | Rightward shift |
| New tax on production | Leftward shift |
| More firms entering the market | Rightward shift |
| Fewer firms (e.g., a big producer closes) | Leftward shift |

Each factor changes the **cost of production** – the amount of money a firm must spend to make each unit.  
When the cost falls, producers can profit at lower prices, so they are willing to supply more.  
When the cost rises, they need higher prices to stay profitable, so they supply less.

> **In daily life:** When smartphones become cheaper to make because a new chip is invented, more phones appear in stores and the price you pay usually goes down.

### Finding the new equilibrium after a supply shift  

1. **Write the new supply equation.**  
   The equation shows quantity supplied ($Q_s$) as a function of price ($P$).  
2. **Keep the demand equation the same** (unless demand also changes).  
3. **Set the two equations equal** because at equilibrium $Q_s = Q_d$.  
4. **Solve for the price $P$** – this is the new market price.  
5. **Plug the price back into either equation** to find the new quantity $Q$.

#### Worked Example  

**Example 5 (Medium): New technology lowers production cost**  

A new technology lowers production cost, shifting supply to  

\[
Q_s = 40 + 3P
\]

The original demand is  

\[
Q_d = 100 - 2P
\]

Find the new equilibrium price and quantity.

1. **Set supply equal to demand.**  
   $$40 + 3P = 100 - 2P$$  

2. **Collect the $P$ terms on one side.**  
   Add $2P$ to both sides: $$40 + 5P = 100$$  

3. **Solve for $P$.**  
   Subtract $40$ from both sides: $$5P = 60$$  
   Divide by $5$: $$P = 12$$  

4. **Find the equilibrium quantity** by substituting $P = 12$ into either equation (use the supply equation).  
   $$Q_s = 40 + 3(12) = 40 + 36 = 76$$  

**Answer:** The new equilibrium price is **$12** per unit, and the equilibrium quantity is **76 units**.  
Because the supply curve moved right, the price fell from its original level (which was $10$ when supply was $20+2P$) and the quantity sold increased.

> **Note:** The direction of the price change tells you whether the shift was an increase (right) or decrease (left) in supply. A rightward shift always pushes price down and quantity up, holding demand constant.

### Quick checklist for a supply shift problem  

- Identify the cause (technology, input price, tax, etc.).  
- Write the new supply equation reflecting the change.  
- Keep the demand equation unchanged unless told otherwise.  
- Equate $Q_s$ and $Q_d$, solve for $P$, then for $Q$.  
- Interpret the result: right shift → lower price, higher quantity; left shift → higher price, lower quantity.

> **Remember:** A supply shift does **not** change the shape of the curve; it merely slides the whole line left or right. The slope (how quickly quantity changes with price) stays the same unless the underlying relationship between price and quantity changes.

With these steps you can handle any situation where technology or input prices move the supply curve, and you will always be able to locate the new market equilibrium.

sections.heading: 6. Combined Shifts and Real‑World Example
sections.body:
When both the demand curve **and** the supply curve move at the same time, the market does not simply “pick one side” and stay there.  
Instead, the new equilibrium price and quantity are found by looking at **how far** each curve shifts.  
If the demand shift is larger than the supply shift, price will tend to rise; if the supply shift is larger, price will tend to fall.  
Quantity, however, always moves in the direction of the larger shift – it rises when either demand or supply expands more than the other, and falls when the opposite happens.

> **Note:** *Shift* means the whole curve moves left (decrease) or right (increase). It is different from a *movement* along a curve, which happens when only price changes.

Think of a busy coffee shop.  
- A new office opens nearby, bringing more customers (demand goes up).  
- At the same time, the coffee bean supplier raises prices, so the shop can afford to buy fewer beans (supply goes down).  

Both changes happen together. The shop will likely raise its coffee price because more people want coffee **and** it has fewer beans to sell. The exact new price depends on which effect is stronger.

### How to analyse combined shifts

1. **Write the new demand and supply equations.**  
   Each equation shows the relationship between price ($P$) and quantity ($Q$).  

2. **Set the two equations equal** to find the equilibrium where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied.  

3. **Solve for the equilibrium price ($P^*$).**  

4. **Plug $P^*$ back into either equation** to get the equilibrium quantity ($Q^*$).  

5. **Compare the size of the shifts** to see which side moved more.  
   - If the new demand curve is farther to the right than the new supply curve is to the left, price rises.  
   - If the new supply curve is farther to the left than the new demand curve is to the right, price falls.  

> **In daily life:** When a popular new smartphone is released (demand up) while a chip shortage limits production (supply down), the phone’s price usually jumps sharply because both forces push price upward.

### Worked Example

**Example 5 (Hard): Drought and Health Trend**

A drought reduces wheat supply to  

\[
Q_s = 10 + 4P
\]

while a health trend raises demand to  

\[
Q_d = 80 - P
\]

Determine the equilibrium price and quantity and explain which effect is stronger.

1. **Set demand equal to supply.**  
   Write the equation that says “quantity demanded = quantity supplied”.  

   $$
   80 - P = 10 + 4P
   $$

2. **Solve for the equilibrium price $P^*$.**  
   Bring the $P$ terms to one side and constants to the other.  

   $$
   80 - 10 = 4P + P \\
   70 = 5P \\
   P^* = \frac{70}{5} = 14
   $$

3. **Find the equilibrium quantity $Q^*$.**  
   Substitute $P^* = 14$ into either the demand or supply equation (both give the same result).  

   Using demand:  

   $$
   Q^* = 80 - P^* = 80 - 14 = 66
   $$

**Answer:** The new equilibrium price is **\$14 per unit**, and the equilibrium quantity is **66 units**.  

The demand shift (from the original demand curve, not shown here, to $Q_d = 80 - P$) moves the curve **rightward**, increasing the quantity people want at every price.  
The supply shift (to $Q_s = 10 + 4P$) moves the curve **leftward**, reducing the quantity producers are willing to sell at every price.  

Because the equilibrium price rose from whatever it was before (the exact previous price is not needed for this conclusion) and the quantity fell compared with the original supply‑only level, we can say **the supply reduction is the stronger effect on quantity**, while **the demand increase pushes price upward**. The net result is a higher price and a lower quantity than before the drought.

### Putting it together

When you face a real‑world situation with simultaneous shifts:

- Write the new equations clearly.  
- Solve step‑by‑step as shown.  
- After you have $P^*$ and $Q^*$, interpret: which curve moved more?  

> **Remember:** *The side that moves farther* determines the direction of the price change, while *the side that expands more* determines whether the quantity rises or falls.

### Quick checklist for combined shifts

- [ ] Identify the cause of each shift (e.g., weather, trends, technology).  
- [ ] Translate each cause into a new demand or supply equation.  
- [ ] Equate the two equations and solve for $P^*$.  
- [ ] Compute $Q^*$ using the found price.  
- [ ] Compare the magnitude of the shifts to explain the direction of change.  

By following these small, ordered steps, you can confidently analyse any market where both buyers and sellers are changing their behavior at the same time. This skill is useful not only in textbooks but also when you read news about housing markets, oil prices, or even the price of concert tickets.

practice.q: What does the law of demand tell us about the relationship between price and quantity demanded?
practice.a: The law of demand says that, all else being equal, when the price of a good goes up, the quantity demanded goes down, and when the price goes down, the quantity demanded goes up. This creates a downward‑sloping demand curve.

practice.q: In your own words, describe what a supply curve shows.
practice.a: A supply curve shows how much of a good producers are willing to sell at different prices. As the price rises, producers are willing to supply more because they can earn higher profits, so the curve slopes upward.

practice.q: Explain how a new technology that makes it cheaper to produce smartphones would affect the supply curve and the market equilibrium price and quantity.
practice.a: The new technology lowers production costs, so producers can supply the same quantity at a lower price, or more quantity at the same price. This shifts the supply curve to the right. With demand unchanged, the rightward shift creates a new equilibrium: the equilibrium price falls and the equilibrium quantity rises.

practice.q: Compare the effect on equilibrium when (a) consumer income rises for a normal good, and (b) a tax is imposed on producers of that good.
practice.a: (a) For a normal good, higher consumer income increases demand, shifting the demand curve right. Equilibrium price and quantity both rise. (b) A tax on producers raises their cost, shifting the supply curve left. Equilibrium price to consumers rises, equilibrium quantity falls. So income increase pushes price up, tax pushes price up but quantity down.

practice.q: A city introduces a rent‑control law that caps apartment rents below the market‑clearing price. Explain, using supply and demand concepts, what happens to the quantity of apartments supplied, the quantity demanded, and any resulting surplus or shortage.
practice.a: Rent control sets a price ceiling below the equilibrium price. At this lower price, the quantity of apartments that landlords are willing to supply falls (movement up the supply curve), while the quantity that renters want to rent rises (movement down the demand curve). The result is that quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied, creating a shortage of apartments.

practice.q: Imagine both a popular new video game and a rise in gamers’ disposable income occur at the same time. Predict how each shift (demand and supply) will affect the equilibrium price and quantity, and explain which effect will dominate if the magnitude of the shifts is unknown.
practice.a: The new video game increases demand for gaming consoles, shifting the demand curve right, which tends to raise both equilibrium price and quantity. The rise in disposable income also shifts demand right (for a normal good), reinforcing the same effect. If supply is unchanged, the combined demand shift will definitely increase price and quantity. If there is also a supply shift (e.g., producers increase output), the net effect on price depends on which shift is larger; however, without a supply change, the dominant effect is the demand increase, leading to higher price and higher quantity.

data.recap: The lesson explains demand as how much consumers want to buy at different prices and supply as how much producers are willing to sell. It introduces demand and supply curves, shows how their intersection determines the equilibrium price and quantity, and describes how shifts in these curves affect the market.
